To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the water companies in nineteenth century London invested in water and sanitation infrastructure to improve water quality, that they were often ahead of the government in improving quality and that government decisions were responsible for the decline of water quality in London.
water companies were continually investing, improving, innovating and expanding during the nineteenth century, and that the government’s role was to encourage, follow and regulate.
water companies were continually innovating and improving water quality in the face of a changing regulatory environment and severe uncertainty about how to improve quality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the processes of innovation, improvement, and regulation that took place in nineteenth-century London and how the government and private sector interacted in the provision of clean water to the city.
how the water companies were able to improve the quality of water supplied to London, in spite of the many problems that they faced.
the role of the state in the development of the water supply system in nineteenth-century London, in particular the role of regulation in the provision of safe drinking water.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
water companies were not as bad as critics have argued, but neither were they as good as they could have been.
government intervention in the water industry in nineteenth century London was not the cause of water quality deterioration, but was a necessary condition for the improvement of water quality.
government intervention was responsible for much of London’s poor water quality in the nineteenth century, but that government intervention also improved quality and access.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
government regulation of London’s water supply during the nineteenth century had a mixed effect on public health.
government intervention, rather than the private water companies, was the major source of poor water quality in London.
the water companies were doing the best they could, given the knowledge they had, to provide clean, safe water to Londoners.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the water companies were not monopolies.
government regulation can be an impediment to improving water quality and that private water companies can play a positive role in providing water and sanitation services.
the private water companies of the nineteenth century were not the villains that they have been made out to be.
